opus-5.5.text:
I think it's incredibly valuable, and honestly it's something I only fully appreciated in hindsight. When I was starting out as a student, I spent a lot of time on things that didn't look like "research" in the glamorous sense. I was writing code, implementing algorithms from scratch, trying to understand why a gradient boosting implementation was slow, or why some matrix operation behaved differently on different hardware. At the time, it sometimes felt like I was just doing engineering. But those foundations turned out to be what let me see problems other people weren't seeing.

Take XGBoost, for example. That project didn't start with me saying, "I want to solve a big open research problem in tree boosting." It came from actually building the system, running into the bottlenecks, and realizing there were real questions about sparsity-aware algorithms, cache-aware access patterns, and distributed computation. Once you have your hands dirty with the system, the research problems almost reveal themselves. You start to notice the gap between what a paper says and what actually happens when you run it on real data at scale.

The same thing happened later with TVM and machine learning compilation. Because I had built systems before, when deep learning frameworks started to proliferate and hardware started to diversify, I could feel the pain point very concretely. How do you take a model and make it run efficiently on a GPU, a phone, an accelerator that didn't exist last year? That question is easy to state, but you really need a foundation in both the machine learning side and the systems side to even know which sub-problems are worth attacking.

So my view is that technical foundations are kind of like a lens. Without them, you can still read papers and find problems, but they're often problems defined by someone else's framing. With strong foundations, you can define your own problems, and you can tell which ones actually matter in practice. I also think it gives you a certain confidence. When you know you can build things end to end, you're not afraid to go after an ambitious direction, because you know that even if the first idea doesn't work, you'll learn something by building it.

That said, I don't think it's an either-or. You shouldn't just build for years in isolation without looking up. The best situation is a kind of loop: you build, you discover problems, you go learn the theory or the techniques needed, and then you build again at a higher level. For me, that cycle between building foundations and discovering problems has been the core of how I do research, and it's something I try to encourage in my students as well.

r001.rationale: He says his early hands-on work building systems and understanding algorithms gave him the foundation to recognize and pursue research problems as they emerged.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think building technical foundations early is actually one of the most underrated things you can do, because it changes what kinds of problems you're even able to see.

When I was a student, I spent a lot of time just writing systems from scratch. Not because I had a specific research question in mind, but because I wanted to understand how things worked all the way down. XGBoost started that way, honestly. I was working on gradient boosting, and I kept running into limits with the existing tools, so I built my own. That experience of building the whole thing, the data structures, the parallelism, the memory layout, gave me an intuition that I couldn't have gotten from reading papers.

And what I found is that once you have that foundation, research problems kind of come to you. You start noticing gaps. You see that the algorithm people want to run doesn't map cleanly onto the hardware, or that the abstraction everyone is using leaks in some important way. Those observations became the seeds for things like MXNet and later TVM. The compiler work in TVM in particular came from sitting at the boundary between machine learning and systems and realizing that nobody was really treating the deployment problem as a first-class research question.

So I'd put it this way. If you jump straight into chasing a broad range of problems without foundations, you tend to work on whatever is popular, and you compete with everyone else on the same ground. If you build depth first, you develop a kind of vantage point that is uniquely yours. The problems you find from there are often ones other people haven't noticed yet, and you're also one of the few people equipped to solve them.

The one caveat I'd add is that foundations shouldn't become a reason to delay forever. The best way I've found is to build something real that people actually use. That forces you to go deep, but it also keeps you connected to what matters. Open source was great for that for me. Users tell you very quickly where your understanding is incomplete.

r001.rationale: The response says that building technical foundations helped Chen notice research problems as they arose and equipped him to solve them.

astra-6.text:
I think building technical foundations is valuable because it gives you the tools to explore. When you encounter a new problem, you can go beyond recognizing that it’s interesting—you can start to understand what makes it difficult and what you might do about it.

But I wouldn’t think of it as a strict sequence where you finish learning the foundations and then discover research problems. The two can reinforce each other. You learn enough to start working on a problem, and that problem reveals gaps in your understanding. Then you go back and learn more, with a clearer sense of why it matters.

So I would build depth while leaving room to explore. A strong foundation helps you make progress, and exposure to different problems helps you decide where that foundation is most useful.

r001.rationale: The response says technical foundations help someone explore and make progress on problems, but it does not state that Tianqi Chen’s earlier training enabled him to tackle research problems as they arose.

sol-6.1.text:
I think building technical foundations gives you the tools to recognize and work on a broader range of problems. When you encounter something new, you can connect it to ideas you already understand, and that helps you figure out where to start.

But I wouldn’t treat it as a strict sequence where you finish learning the foundations and then begin looking for research problems. Working on a concrete problem often shows you which foundations you’re missing. So the two reinforce each other: you build enough depth to make progress, explore, and then go back and learn more as the problem demands.
